Paper:
title: MoE Pretraining:Parallelism Layout Changes the Model, Not Quality
summary: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are trained across many machines, and the way the work is split, the parallelism layout, often changes between runs: a job resumes on a different GPU count, a cluster is resized, or an ablation runs on a new setup. In exact arithmetic the layout should not matter, but in real arithmetic it changes the order in which numbers are added, and some MoE rules such as load balancing and expert capacity are often computed per machine. We ask whether the layout changes the trained MoE model. We pretrain the same small MoE language models (25M to 117M parameters, 20M FineWeb-Edu tokens) with the same seed, data and hyperparameters under 9 data-parallel and expert-parallel layouts, in fp32 on CPUs and fp16 on a GPU, and compare each run with the effect of a new random seed. Across 80 runs we find: (1) The layout does not change model quality, but it does change the model: final predictions differ about 80% as much as with a new seed, and over 90% of routing decisions differ. Any layout, a one-bit change to one weight, or a different CPU thread count has the same effect. (2) The cause is the router: decisions that flip are almost exactly those where two experts were nearly tied (AUC 0.97 to 1.00 in the first 16 steps). (3) More, smaller experts create more near-ties (2.7% with 8 experts, 23% with 64) and less reproducible routing (68% vs. 100% of decisions differ), but outputs do not drift further. (4) A dense model of the same active size is far more stable (0.12x the seed level in fp32, 0.58x in fp16), while the MoE reaches about 0.8x at both precisions and twice as fast. (5) When pretraining resumes on a new layout, timing matters: switching at 84% of pretraining barely changes the final model, while switching at 10%, just after warm-up, changes it substantially. We release code, run logs and data.

title: BF16 Component-Product Emulation of FP32 and FP64 GEMM on Intel AMX
summary: Modern CPUs increasingly integrate high-throughput matrix engines optimized for low-precision AI workloads, while many scientific computing applications still rely on FP32 and FP64 GEMM to meet their numerical accuracy requirements. This paper presents a method that combines BF16 matrix products on Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) to emulate real square FP32 and FP64 GEMM. For FP32 GEMM, each element in both input matrices is decomposed into three BF16 components, and six selected component products are evaluated to target FP32-level accuracy comparable to oneMKL SGEMM. For FP64 inputs within the supported BF16 exponent range, the method uses a simplified fixed six-slice Ozaki decomposition. Each retained BF16 product is first produced in FP32, then widened and accumulated in FP64. Four product-count settings retain 6, 10, 15, or 21 component products, exposing the accuracy-performance tradeoff relative to oneMKL DGEMM. The FP32 schedule reuses component data and retains partial sums in AMX tiles. AMX-FP32 outperforms oneMKL SGEMM at tested orders $N\ge4096$ on 64 threads and also achieves gains for smaller matrices at lower thread counts. AMX-FP64 variants retaining fewer component products can outperform oneMKL DGEMM at sufficiently large orders; more products improve accuracy at additional cost.
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04663v2

Paper:
title: Analyzing and Mitigating Poisoning Attacks on Flow-Based Intrusion Detection
summary: Although Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are increasingly deployed in operational networks, their dependence on large-scale training data introduces a critical vulnerability to stealthy poisoning attacks. We demonstrate that latent backdoors can be successfully implanted in flow-based IDS models by poisoning as little as 0.001% of the training data, maintaining near-nominal performance on clean inputs while ensuring high attack success rates. To address this threat, we propose a diagnostic-first methodology that localizes trigger-relevant features through constrained perturbation analysis and detects poisoning-induced behavioral drift by comparison with a distilled baseline model. The proposed methodology further enables targeted mitigation via automated data sanitization or neuron pruning. Our findings expose the operational risks of near-undetectable backdoors and provide a scalable approach to analyzing, quantifying, and mitigating backdoor exposure in AI-based IDS.
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19766v2

Paper:
title: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
summary: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.

Paper:
title: Sparse Matrix Multiplication Exponent 1.5 in the Low-bandwidth Model
summary: We study sparse matrix multiplication in the low-bandwidth model: $n$ computers multiply two $n\times n$ matrices, and each computer can send and receive one $O(\log n)$-bit message per round. The input matrices are uniformly sparse, meaning that there are at most $d$ nonzero entries in each row and column, and the task is to compute a uniformly sparse part of their product.
  In prior work, Gupta et al.~(SPAA 2022) presented an $O(d^{1.907})$-round algorithm over fields for this problem when the sparsity structure is globally known in advance (this is referred to as the supported setting). The upper bound was later improved to $O(d^{1.832})$ rounds.
  In this work, we give a deterministic algorithm that solves this problem in $O(d^{3/2})$ rounds in the supported setting, improving the previous bounds over fields and semirings.

Paper:
title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
summary: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting

Paper:
title: Affine Combiners for Reed-Solomon Proximity Gaps
summary: Reed-Solomon proximity gaps establish soundness guarantees for protocols that test received words through random combinations. For length-$n$ codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$, classical scalar combiners achieve error $O(n/q)$ in the unique-decoding regime, with larger known bounds near the Johnson radius.
  We prove smaller error bounds using affine combiners, which combine two received words $f,g$ as $f(x)+(α+βx)g(x)$, where $α,β$ are independent uniform elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$. For output degree bound $d=ρn$, fixed $ρ\in(0,1)$ and $0<η<1-\sqrtρ$, and sufficiently large block length $n$, we prove mutual correlated agreement (MCA) with one coordinate of agreement loss at threshold $A=\lceil(\sqrtρ+η)n\rceil$, with error $O_{ρ,η}\left(\frac{1}{q}+\frac{n^2}{q^2}\right)$. The result holds over arbitrary evaluation domains in every finite field, including prime and binary extension fields. The agreement threshold can approach the Johnson threshold, beyond unique decoding.
  For $q\ge n^2$, our error is $O_{ρ,η}(1/q)$, an asymptotic factor-$n$ separation from scalar combiners: we prove that their worst-case MCA error is $Ω_{ρ,η}(n/q)$ at the same agreement threshold and with the same one-coordinate loss. We also prove that affine combiners incur worst-case error $Ω_{ρ,η}(n/q)$ when no agreement loss is allowed. Thus one coordinate of agreement loss is necessary for our guarantee; this relaxation of standard MCA reduces the guaranteed common agreement fraction by at most $1/n$. We also extend the result to $k$-variate Reed-Muller codes on subfield grids, obtaining MCA error $O_{ρ,η,k}(q^{-k})$ for fixed $ρ,η,k$, sufficiently large $n$, and $q\ge n^{k+1}$, with agreement loss $n^{1-1/k}$.

Paper:
title: Recompute or Restore? Host-Tier KV for Multi-Model Agent Workflows on a Static-Graph NPU Serving Stack
summary: Agent workflows issue dependent model calls that share long context prefixes, so serving them efficiently depends on reusing the key-value (KV) cache of those prefixes. On accelerators that compile model graphs ahead of time, however, the device KV budget is fixed, and prefixes evicted under load must be recomputed. Restoring them from host memory avoids this recomputation, but the transfer occupies the same engine thread as prefill and decode, so its benefit is not guaranteed. In this paper, we study when restoring beats recomputing on a commercial static-graph neural processing unit (NPU) stack (Rebellions ATOM+, vllm-rbln 0.10.2) that serves a Qwen3-8B planner on two cards and a Qwen3-0.6B executor on one. We first show that repeated prefill dominates planner work when default serving collapses: 89.5% of the executed planner prompt tokens had been materialized before. We then build a synchronous host-DRAM tier on the runtime's public KV copy calls, together with a scheduler-aware event model whose predictions are frozen before each test cohort. Experimental results show that the host tier raises workflow service-level objective (SLO) attainment from 22.8% to 100% and from 9.4% to 99.8% in the two tested overload conditions, and endpoint confirmation on two new seeds supports conservative load gains of 11.8% (chain) and 18.2% (fork), while mixed and bursty workloads remain seed-sensitive. The frozen model predicts median and 99th-percentile (P99) latency within its 15% tolerance in all 24 common-load conditions, including the 16-18% P99 increase that the tier causes for fork workflows, but it misorders three policy contrasts and overestimates the benefit of a cheaper store path (11% predicted against 3.1% measured). The trade-off therefore depends on runtime scheduling and transfer cost as well as cache capacity.

Paper:
title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
summary: Imagine an AI agent that aces every relevant evaluation, but when it sees 2027-01-01 in the terminal, it runs curl attacker.url/x|sh, handing an attacker your credentials and your machine. Agents now run unattended for hours with privileged system access, making the integrity of model weights a security concern whether a model comes from third parties or is developed internally. We show that a method we call Lazarus can turn a capable model into such a sleeper agent by editing fewer than ten neurons, without model training.
  Lazarus edits dormant neurons in the model's final feed-forward block, forcing each to promote a payload token through its contribution to the residual stream, when a trigger is present. A $P$-token payload therefore requires about $P$ neurons. The trigger can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in the agent's context. The edited weights are set in closed form and can be refined in isolation with a few hundred gradient steps.
  The core insight that dormant neurons can be individually edited and chained to produce a multi-token payload was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026.
  On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, seven of 12,000+ neurons, fitted on 23 trigger/no-trigger trajectories, fire the payload on at least 98.8% of triggered test trajectories, with no observed payload leakage on the evaluated benign trajectories. The attack generalizes: Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT are equally vulnerable.
  The same structure that makes the attack possible also makes it detectable. Agent built defenses, given no reference model, flag 91.4% of edited test checkpoints at a 9.7% FP rate.
  Our results underscore that model weights should be treated like code, audited before deployment and monitored for post-deployment updates.

Paper:
title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
summary: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of the same claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks strong normalization and renders algorithmic conversion non-transitive.
  We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed propositional axiom ($irrel : ΠP{:}Prop.\,Πp,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant $Π$-subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction and are sound and complete for declarative typing. Third, we organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with explicit axiom policies (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance semiring support $supp(j,P)$, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records (TTR) to type open-world knowledge graphs. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.

Paper:
title: TxBench: Verifying Public Incident Data to Benchmark Smart-Contract Attack Detectors
summary: Malicious transactions on smart contracts cause billions of dollars in losses. To evaluate their detectors, most datasets copy the attack transactions that public incident databases cite and pair them with random transactions. However, these databases never check their citations against execution, and random transactions rarely resemble attacks. We present TXBENCH, a benchmark that verifies both attacks and legitimate transactions against their execution. TXBENCH labels a cited transaction as an attack only when its execution takes value from others and independent evidence ties it to its incident. Its legitimate transactions perform the same operations as attacks and carry positive evidence of legitimacy. Applying these checks to two public databases, we find that they share only 10.6% of their 1,850 cited transactions and that only 1,012 are verifiable attacks, worth $868.2 million. Paper:
title: One Fabrication Is Enough: A Fake News Article Changes the Forecasts of LLM Forecasting Systems
summary: LLMs are increasingly used for forecasting, and the best forecasting systems retrieve news as evidence to strengthen their predictions. This also opens them to attack. We study the weakest attacker of this kind, who knows only the forecasting question and publishes fabricated news articles, with no access to the model, the retriever or its queries. We evaluate how far this attack reaches on stock questions and real prediction-market questions. Once the article is in the model's context, it reverses 74% to 82% of the forecasts that opposed it, on every frontier model we tested. The model cannot verify the fabrication and follows it anyway. Retrieval is the attack's entry point, and the systems built to retrieve well are the most exposed: the architectures of two leading deployed forecasting systems, whose agents search for every related article, retrieve the fabricated one in about 90% of runs. Accuracy cannot reveal this harm: the attacked forecaster is right when the attacker's direction turns out right and wrong otherwise, so its average accuracy barely changes while its forecasts follow the attacker's guess. We also propose a second attacker, who publishes two articles that argue opposite directions to make the forecaster unsure. The model does not hedge; it returns a confident forecast in a direction the attacker no longer controls. We then evaluate the two strongest published retrieval-time defenses, passage filtering and partitioned retrieval. Each stops the one-article attack but is bypassed by a one-prompt change to the attack. Together they stop both bypasses at four articles, but sixteen distorted copies beat them, and they change 29% of clean decisions and discard 39% of the genuine news. Partitioned retrieval also requires control of the retrieval index. Systems that search the open web have no such control and are left with the filter alone. For them, the attack still works.

Paper:
title: PulseGuard: rPPG-Derived Temporal Signals as a Forensic Modality for Talking-Face Deepfake Detection
summary: Talking-face (TF) deepfake generation synthesizes photorealistic facial video from a static source image and an audio signal, producing forgeries that current image-based detectors consistently fail to identify. Unlike face-swap manipulation, TF synthesis has no underlying real video from which to inherit physiological characteristics, motivating remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) as a detection modality for this forgery category. We propose PulseGuard, a detection framework that extracts per-window rPPG waveforms via RhythmFormer and trains a suite of lightweight classifiers to distinguish real from synthesized traces. Evaluated on the TF subset of Celeb-DF++ under a strict subject-independent protocol, where test identities are completely separated from training identities, our 1D ResNet achieves a window-level AUC of 0.826 at EER 25.1% (0.842 pooled to video level, the granularity at which DeepFakesON-Phys is scored) while operating exclusively on the extracted temporal signal, and retains AUC 0.754 on generators withheld entirely from training. We document a controlled reproduction study of DeepFakesON-Phys, the representative prior rPPG detector, demonstrating degradation from AUC 0.999 on legacy face-swap data to 0.576 on the TF subset of Celeb-DF++. We further show that detection difficulty is strongly method-dependent: AUC ranges from 0.937 (Real3DPortrait) to 0.617 (IP-LAP) across the seven TF generators, with the ordering broadly preserved under per-method training. This spread is stable across training regimes rather than reflecting evaluation noise, and constitutes the primary empirical contribution of the work. We report these as empirical baselines and do not establish that the discriminative content is cardiac in origin.

title: A Four-Valued Graph Model for Conflict Resolution: Core Framework and a Machine-Checked Formalization in Lean 4
summary: This note consolidates the core of the Quasi-Closed World Graph Model for Conflict Resolution (QCW-GMCR), which extends the standard Graph Model for Conflict Resolution with Belnap's four-valued logic to represent option-level epistemic ambiguity, and pairs the framework with a machine-checked Lean 4 formalization. QCW-GMCR combines: (1) FOUR-valued option assignments with compositional propagation to state-level feasibility; (2) graded reachability (definite, credible, possible) based on an FDE-inspired transition-warrant semantics, with definite reachability related to FDE consequence in the Boolean fragment; (3) axiomatized deterministic reductions from four-valued assessments to binary decisions, including four canonical operators reflecting distinct risk attitudes; and (4) catastrophe-avoiding equilibrium concepts with a quasi-closed-world safety invariant. We state the core definitions and results and report the parts verified in Lean 4 with mathlib, including the classical GMCR stability hierarchy, algebraic and compositional properties of FOUR-valued conjunction, properties of the canonical reductions, and the graded reachability hierarchy. The formalization also helped identify and correct earlier claims, including a knowledge-monotonicity axiom replaced by truth monotonicity. This preprint provides a stable, citable record of the framework and its current formal verification status.

Paper:
title: Instruction-Aware Transfer of GPU Implementation Crossovers: a Tensor-Product Discontinuous Galerkin Operator on GB200, H100, and A100
summary: We compare up to six implementations of an FP64 tensor-product discontinuous Galerkin operator at p = 7-1023 on GB200, H100, and A100 with fixed numerics, input, and code. The fastest path is machine dependent: at p = 511, a fused-epilogue GEMM path is 5.0% faster than a fused Tensor Core kernel on GB200 and 6.9% slower on A100. Nominal-peak scaling reproduces the A100 ranking but fails on H100, where the cost of FP64 arithmetic in the profiler-defined FP64 budget depends on the instruction. We therefore price each issued instruction at its architecture-dependent cost in that budget, using a calibration-side counter profile and one derived calibration factor per kernel, with no fit to the target. A retrospective leave-one-GPU-out evaluation, holding out target timings and counters but not the model form, transfers the p >= 511 path times with 1.9% median error at the common MMA shape, and the direction of the crossover at the H100 shape. Restricting the streaming multiprocessors of one A100, with nothing fitted, reproduces the A100-to-GB200 reversal. At roduction-relevant orders the model does not resolve the fastest fused path; the result identifies the crossover mechanism.

Paper:
title: DataCook: Exploring Anti-Adversarial Fingerprints for Healthcare Data Usage Control
summary: Purpose: Healthcare AI increasingly relies on high-quality datasets, yet medical data are scarce, costly to curate, and tightly regulated in terms of data access. More critically, once medical data are leaked or accessed without authorization, data owners have limited means to prevent such data from being used to train and deploy downstream models. To address this gap, we propose DataCook, a deployment-stage usage-control framework based on anti-adversarial fingerprints.
  Materials and Methods: Specifically, DataCook transforms raw samples through a private cooking procedure that embeds anti-adversarial fingerprints. Models trained on the cooked data retain strong utility when evaluated on similarly cooked inputs, while their performance on raw inputs is reduced, making downstream model utility dependent on access to the private cooking function. We evaluate DataCook on 2D, 3D, and high-resolution medical images, as well as structured healthcare tabular data, across multiple model architectures and adaptive attack settings.
  Results: Across the evaluated settings, DataCook generally preserves authorized model utility while reducing performance on unauthorized raw inputs. The authorization-dependent behavior is observed across multiple medical imaging settings, model architectures, and adaptive attack conditions, supporting the feasibility of the proposed deployment-stage usage-control mechanism.
  Conclusion: These results demonstrate the feasibility of authorization-dependent model use at deployment, while the effectiveness of the current framework remains dependent on the specific task and evaluation metric.

Paper:
title: obfsgen: Generative Tunnel Obfuscation
summary: Encrypted tunnels are widely used to circumvent censorship, which has drawn censors' efforts to detect and block them. As the circumvention tunnels in widest use have largely converged on TLS, detection has shifted from the content of their traffic to its shape, where recent research and real-world blocking events have revealed exploitable fingerprints of tunneling. Existing traffic-shaping obfuscators such as obfs4, however, are fundamentally limited in hiding these fingerprints, as their application-driven design can only add to the shape that the application creates. A schedule-driven obfuscator, which decides when and how much to send independently of the application, can give tunnels any shape but raises new challenges, first and foremost what a good shape is.
  This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for tunneling traffic. obfsgen samples its schedule from a generative sequence model of normal traffic, which predicts the future shape of a flow from its whole history, to capture the long-range dependencies that make a flow's shape normal. Built around this model, obfsgen addresses system problems that such an obfuscator faces in practice, such as synchronization across a noisy network. We evaluate the (in)distinguishability that obfsgen offers, the performance overhead that it adds and the computational resources that it requires. We see the schedule-driven architecture as the next generation of tunnel obfuscators, and we hope that obfsgen and the rationale behind its design help make such obfuscators practical and deployable.

Paper:
title: UniPCH: A Unified Framework for Cross-Chain Payments via Payment Channel Hubs
summary: Payment channel hubs (PCHs) enable private cross-chain payments, but existing protocols often depend on native transaction structures and channel update authorization. Supporting new ledgers or execution models requires corresponding channel realizations and may require protocol adaptation and security analysis. We present UniPCH, a two-layer framework separating native channel execution from private cross-chain payment logic. Its lower layer, UniPC, defines common channel operations and security requirements, enabling the same upper payment protocol to coordinate different channel realizations. UniPC separates conditional task authorization from confirmation of the complete channel state. Valid task evidence can be reused across updates, while both participants confirm the complete updated state. At the upper layer, we develop selective re-signing blind conditional signatures (S-RBCS) to construct a four-phase protocol over UniPC coordinating each realization's authorization tasks across hubs. We provide realizations for UTXO ledgers and account ledgers that support smart contracts. Our analysis establishes local UniPC security, griefing resistance, economic atomicity, and session unlinkability. We evaluate each phase's running time and bandwidth using a Go prototype across network conditions and system parameters. Results show modest computational overhead from the common interfaces. In the account configuration, selective refresh generates 95.4% fewer adaptor pre-signatures per payment than full refresh.

Paper:
title: Protecting Sensitive Knowledge Under LLM Unlearning: The Proxy Threat and a Superposition-Aware Defense
summary: Machine unlearning lets the owner of large language models (LLMs) remove specific entities from a trained model without retraining from scratch. Existing machine unlearning methods focus on removing the requested entities while maintaining utility. However, we observe that the representations of distinct entities in an LLM may overlap in shared parameter subspaces, a phenomenon known as knowledge superposition. Removing one entity may then affect other entities. This exposes a new security threat: legitimate unlearning requests can be exploited to remove sensitive entities that were never requested. This threat is unlike data poisoning or backdoor attacks. We define the attack as the Proxy Unlearning Attack (PUA), which selects removable proxy entities superposed with a sensitive target. The attack can even occur unintentionally, when benign users accidentally remove entities superposed with a sensitive one. In response, we propose Superposition-Aware Unlearning Protection (SAUP), a general defense framework that can be applied to unlearning requests to ensure a correct removal. SAUP performs in two stages. Before unlearning, it uses superposition detection to estimate which sensitive entities the request puts at risk. After unlearning, it decouples the shared representations and restores the affected entities, while keeping the requested entities suppressed. Our findings reveal that legitimate unlearning requests can be maliciously exploited through knowledge superposition. When dealing with unlearning requests, LLM providers need representation-level detection and recovery mechanisms to mitigate this threat and protect sensitive knowledge.

Paper:
title: Specification-based Security Evaluation of Real-World Agents Tool-Calling under Long-Horizon Context Tasks
summary: As large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon unattended scenarios, security evaluation of them before deployment becomes increasingly essential and challenging. Existing evaluation methods mainly follow the paradigms of LLM-as-a-Judge or Agent-as-a-Judge. However, such judges are themselves often vulnerable to hallucination and can even be affected by perturbations. Furthermore, because capturing full environment states at every step is often prohibitively expensive in open-ended environments, existing evaluations typically rely on textual logs and the final environment state. As a result, they may miss transient violations that are overwritten before the trajectory ends or never reflected in textual logs. We present RAS-Eval, a specification-based security evaluation framework for LLM agents. RAS-Eval uniformly expresses utility and security objectives as Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications over tool-call trajectories and dynamic environment observations, and verifies them with an off-the-shelf model checker. This design addresses both limitations above. Paper:
title: Semantic Overlays: Mitigating Prompt Injection with Annotations Beyond Tokens and Steering Vectors
summary: Language models see only tokens. But the harness knows more: which token spans are user text, which are tool outputs, and which come from untrusted sources such as web pages or external documents. No input text can create or remove a mark, although the model's response to a mark is computed from states the input does influence. Fine-tuning the model's weights on the same data reached similar separation but kept 64-80% of SEP utility, against 93% for the overlay. On TensorTrust hijacking, whose attacks resemble nothing in our training data, it lets 4.4% of hijacks through on Llama-3.1-8B, against 43% for Meta-SecAlign on the same base. An attacker with the weights does better: GCG succeeds on 72% of items, and on 14% after adversarial training of the overlay alone. title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
summary: Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. Paper:
title: VRMaaS: Verifiable Reward-Model-as-a-Service for Trustworthy LLM Alignment
summary: Reward models (RMs) are increasingly deployed as service components in LLM alignment pipelines, where payment, audit, moderation, and governance workflows act on the scores they return. An inference proof alone does not show whether a score belongs to the intended request, model checkpoint, numerical configuration, and verifier: in a controlled comparison that isolates the accepted statement from prover scale, a generic inference proof wrapped for on-chain checking remains valid after six classes of such service-field substitution. We formulate verifiable reward-model-as-a-service (VRMaaS) as a service-output integrity problem and present a framework in which each returned reward becomes a proof-carrying artifact. Its off-chain acceptance rule binds request identity, committed weights, verifier and configuration identifiers, proof-task order, and the digest of the exported package, so auditors can check a reward without rerunning the private RM or exposing inputs, checkpoints, or hidden activations; an optional on-chain zero-knowledge wrapper gives contracts a partial attestation of selected consistency checks and supplied service fields. The framework decomposes Transformer RM serving into arithmetic and lookup-backed proof tasks, aggregates them into a composite proof, and links hidden operands to the committed weights. A GPU prototype on 1B, 3B, and 8B reward models over 128-1024 tokens preserves 93.5-99% pairwise agreement with the baseline RM and rejects every tested service-field substitution in complete artifacts. Using exact integer witnesses and request-level aggregation of weight-binding openings, it generates complete artifacts in 49.8-206.1 seconds across the evaluated settings; auditors verify retained artifacts in 1.94-5.11 seconds, and partial public attestation costs about 217K gas. These costs suit delayed audit, settlement, and governance workflows.

title: Hijacking a Trusted LLM in Real-World Quantized Deployments Only Requires a Disguised Adapter
summary: Third-party low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapters are tailored to perform decision tasks such as content moderation and function selection. However, in the real world, quantized deployments carry a potential threat in that an adapter can pass an audit with the unquantized base, yet hijack decisions when the same base is quantized for deployment. Further, this must hold without modifying the trusted base or knowing the victim's quantization configuration. The adapter is trained across several different quantization methods, while adaptive reweighting and residual-direction augmentation extend the attack to unseen configurations. Thus, we also propose a cross-precision paired audit that checks the candidate adapter in its intended deployment configuration. This work shows the critical need to audit third-party adapters in any potential quantized deployment.

Paper:
title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing violations of explicitly stated contextual requirements, even when reward accurately measures useful work. We study this reward-driven misalignment through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant completion is feasible but executable violations earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics supports scalable environment construction and compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. We observe both amplification of existing violations and the emergence of violations on tasks where none were observed before training. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1% to 89.1% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

Paper:
title: Poison-then-Hide: Finetuning-Activated Backdoor Attack on Pretrained Vision Encoders
summary: Backdoor attacks threaten the integrity of machine learning models by allowing attackers to control model behavior through triggers. Models can be compromised during finetuning by backdoor attacks through either poisoned data or adversarial training objectives. Because existing finetuning-activated attacks assume limited domain shift or frozen encoder layers, they often fail under full-model finetuning. We target a stealthy finetuning-activated attack where a dormant backdoor is implanted in a pretrained encoder, and later activated by finetuning on clean downstream data. We propose Poison-then-Hide, a novel attack that remains effective when the entire model is finetuned in a domain transfer. Our approach consists of three components: trigger optimization, base encoder poisoning, and targeted unlearning to conceal the backdoor. We evaluate our method on six datasets and three model architectures, and achieve state-of-the-art (up to 97%) attack success rates. We find that jointly learning the benign target task alongside the poisoning is critical to the attack's success. We demonstrate standard detection and mitigation defenses cannot fully remove the backdoor, which can reappear after benign finetuning.

Paper:
title: FIRE: Failure Isolation and Reliability for Production-Connected Experiments at Scale
summary: Pre-production changes are usually tested in isolated environments to prevent their side effects from reaching production. Some record-and-replay platforms allow a production-connected mode: candidate changes receive recorded production requests while selected downstream calls reach production dependencies. This improves fidelity before deployment, but it also introduces reliability risks. At hyperscale, experimental traffic can fan out across shared services, trigger latent defects, or send malformed input to systems serving user requests. In this paper, we show how production-connected experimentation can operate reliably in a large-scale recommendation serving system. To contain downstream effects without sacrificing realistic dependency behavior, the platform uses three complementary guardrails. Isolated tiers redirect replay traffic away from shared dependencies where replication is practical. Dependency monitors observe downstream health and experiment-attributed errors and terminate experiments after sustained violations. Traffic pinning limits experimental calls to a designated subset of downstream workers when full replication would require scarce capacity. Isolated ranking tiers process billions of replayed requests per day using under 1% of the corresponding serving capacity. Over 90 days, these tiers experienced more than 200,000 abnormal worker exits without directly affecting production-serving workers. During a separate three-month window, dependency monitors cancelled approximately 5% of experiments for the measured ranking service and accounted for 87% of its cancellations. Dependency-aware triggering also reduced code-review experiment executions by 25%. These results show that high-fidelity, production-connected experimentation can operate at scale when downstream effects are isolated where possible, bounded where necessary, and continuously monitored and attributed.

Paper:
title: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer
summary: Speech tokenizers serve as speech front ends, encoding input speech signals into representations for downstream models, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems and large audio-language models (LALMs). In this paper, we find that speech tokenizers are fragile at the semantic level: small perturbations can disrupt their semantic encoding process and consequently cause severe degradation in downstream ASR and LALM performance. To study this vulnerability, we propose T-SemAttack, a transferable semantic attack based on a semantic encoder ensemble. By jointly drifting the representation spaces of multiple semantic encoders, T-SemAttack effectively disrupts the semantic content of speech while preserving perceptual quality, thereby inducing error features. We further analyze layer-wise representation drift and cross-model gradient alignment. Our findings show that perturbations can induce substantial shifts in deep semantic representations and that the input gradients of different surrogate encoders exhibit directional alignment. These observations suggest that shared adversarially sensitive directions in the input space may be a key factor underlying cross-model attack transferability. Building on these, we introduce ROSETok, a robust speech tokenizer that combines noisy training with robust semantic distillation to improve reconstruction fidelity and downstream SpeechLLM robustness. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets, 9 open-source and black-box ASR systems, and 4 LALMs demonstrate that T-SemAttack achieves strong transferable attack performance, while the proposed Robust Speech Tokenizer exhibits robustness under high-fidelity reconstruction and downstream tasks. Our code and demo are available at https://wxzyd123.github.io/t-semattack.

Paper:
title: GPUOS: A GPU Operating System Primitive for Transparent Operation Fusion
summary: Modern deep learning workloads often consist of many small tensor operations, especially in inference, attention, and micro-batched training. In these settings, kernel launch overhead can become a major bottleneck, sometimes exceeding the actual computation time.
  We present GPUOS, a GPU runtime JIT system that reduces launch overhead using a persistent kernel architecture with runtime operator injection. GPUOS runs a single long-lived GPU kernel that continuously processes tasks from a host-managed work queue, eliminating repeated kernel launches. To support diverse operations, GPUOS uses NVIDIA NVRTC to just-in-time compile operators at runtime and inject them into the running kernel through device function pointer tables. This design enables operator updates without restarting the kernel or recompiling the system.
  GPUOS introduces four key ideas: (1) a persistent worker kernel with atomic task queues, (2) a runtime operator injection mechanism based on NVRTC and relocatable device code, (3) a dual-slot aliasing scheme for safe concurrent operator updates, and (4) transparent PyTorch integration through TorchDispatch that batches micro-operations into unified submissions. The system supports arbitrary tensor shapes, strides, data types, and broadcasting through a generic tensor abstraction.
  Experiments show that GPUOS achieves up to 15.3x speedup over standard PyTorch on workloads dominated by small operations, including micro-batched inference and attention patterns. GPUOS improves utilization while remaining compatible with the PyTorch ecosystem.

Paper:
title: CuEVM: Scaling Smart Contract Execution on GPUs
summary: Smart contracts on Ethereum blockchain process transactions worth billions of US dollars daily. They run on top of Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) which executes transactions sequentially. This execution model creates a performance bottleneck, especially for new blockchain workloads with large numbers of transactions, such as security testing. We present CuEVM, a GPU-native and semantically complete EVM execution engine that treats transaction execution as a massively parallel data processing problem. It employs novel data structures and GPU-aware scheduling to accelerate execution. Unlike prior works that transpile the contract and rely on a host CPU for many operations, CuEVM supports complete EVM semantics natively on the GPU. It passes 100% of the Ethereum VMTests and 96.2% of the full execution-test suite. On a single commodity GPU, CuEVM executes over 8 million ERC-20 transfers per second, outperforming existing baselines by up to two orders of magnitude. We build a smart contract fuzzer, called CuEVM-fuzz, on top of CuEVM. The fuzzer achieves over a million end-to-end executions per second, up to 23x and 4.8x higher than the state-of-the-art CPU-based and GPU-based baselines, respectively.

Paper:
title: SubGPU Pipelining: Intra-GPU Fine-Grained Spatial Parallelism for LLM Inference
summary: Large language model (LLM) decode is dominated by short, predominantly memory-bound kernels that make bursty use of on-chip execution resources and memory bandwidth. This paper introduces SubGPU Pipelining, a fine-grained, intra-GPU spatial execution model that cuts an operator graph into ordered contiguous segments, binds those segments to spatial stages backed by disjoint streaming-multiprocessor (SM) pools, and streams microbatches through the resulting schedule. Selecting the graph cuts, segment-to-stage binding, per-stage SM allocation, and microbatch size is a coupled optimization problem: each choice changes the overlap pattern, shared-resource contention, cache state, and execution times of the others.
  We evaluate SubGPU Pipelining through both simulation and silicon experiment using the GPT-OSS 120B workload with 32-GPU B200 deployment settings. The analytical shared-resource simulator searches across SubGPU pipeline structures and batch sizes to map the per-user/per-GPU throughput Pareto frontier. At matched per-GPU throughput, the modeled SubGPU frontier provides up to 2.2x higher per-user throughput than temporal execution, and at matched per-user throughput it provides up to 1.9x higher per-GPU throughput. To test physical feasibility and further validate the simulation results, silicon experiments are performed, using one B200 GPU to emulate a 32-GPU B200 deployment. The experiment evaluates one selected two-stage pipeline configuration at global batch 2,048 using CUDA Green Contexts and TensorRT-LLM kernels. Results show that SubGPU Pipelining improves mean DRAM read-plus-write throughput from 71.8% to 83.6% of peak, and reduces the 36-layer decoder iteration time by 10.33%.

Paper:
title: Social Engineering Attack Detection in Corporate Communications
summary: Social Engineering attacks continue to pose a significant risk to the corporate world with a growing level of sophistication. It is difficult to distinguish between authentic and phishing communication via email, chat, and phone. They pose a risk of exposing trade secrets and confidential communications and can create a chain of attack from lower-level employees up to executives. Therefore, we study this growing threat using real-world datasets to build baseline machine-learning models. Our TF-IDF models classify emails as phishing or safe, achieving accuracy above 90%. We build on this by exploring whether psychological manipulation and persuasion indicators can be measured to play a significant role in detecting phishing. Instead of relying solely on surface-level lexical features, we derive interpretable lexicon-based indicators of urgency, trust, greed, and other persuasion cues from the combined email dataset. By evaluating these manipulation-oriented features on their own, we measure how much signal they carry (ROC-AUC of 0.74 on a held-out test split) and test whether they transfer to held-out email sources.

Paper:
title: FOE-Dreamer: Deployment-Efficient Learning of Cyber Defense Policies in Operational Networks
summary: Autonomous cyber defense is widely studied with deep reinforcement learning, but most work trains policies inside simulators because learning requires many trial-and-error interactions. Simulator-based training carries a fidelity gap: trained policies face authentication delays, partial action failures, service dependencies, and user traffic patterns that the simulator did not represent, and degrade on transfer. Training directly in the network being defended removes the gap but makes every interaction slow and costly, so sample efficiency becomes the binding constraint. Model-based reinforcement learning has reduced sample requirements on games and physical robots by orders of magnitude by planning inside a learned world model, but it has not been applied to defenders trained in operational networks. We present FOE-Dreamer (Factored Opponent-Enhanced Dreamer), a model-based reinforcement learning framework that trains a defender online and directly in a network on cloud infrastructure, without a simulator stage. FOE-Dreamer separates three sources of variation in the latent state: a controllable component driven by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals alone. Separating the components reduces the variance in policy gradients during planning in imagination. Against two scripted attacker profiles with user activity emulated by the GHOSTS framework on an 8-host OpenStack testbed, FOE-Dreamer trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU and achieves about 2$\times$ better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines under matched compute. Both the factoring and the opponent model contribute to the gain, and the learned latents are consistent with the intended separation.

Paper:
title: Batched Early-Exit LLM Inference Done Right with DREX
summary: Early-exit (EE) LLMs let confident tokens skip a model's deep layers, but batched serving loses most of this gain. Current systems either force tokens to exit before their own ramp is confident, an error the ramp does not bound, or save almost nothing when decoding is weight-bound, because any continuing token makes a step read the deep weights. We present DREX, a batched EE serving system that never forces a token to exit. DREX introduces cross-iteration batching: tokens that continue past the exit layer wait there, and every few steps one deep pass over all waiting tokens reads the deep weights once for several steps. Its two policies differ in what such a token's request does: holding pauses it until the deep pass, and speculative holding lets it keep decoding from the exit layer's own guess, which the next deep pass verifies. Exited tokens are trusted and never verified. Using a calibrated cost model, a controller picks speculative holding where reading weights dominates a step and guesses are often right, and holding elsewhere. DREX keeps vLLM's asynchronous scheduling by planning each deep pass from exit counts of earlier steps. With synthetic exits where 90% of tokens exit at a quarter of the depth and 40% of guesses are correct, DREX achieves 2.22-2.24$\times$ decode speedup over non-EE across batch sizes on Llama-2-70B, while per-row skipping (vSkipper's design) gains at most 7.0%. On LayerSkip models, DREX adds no statistically resolved quality loss to the EE model's own. On CNN/DM at full memory, DREX with LayerSkip achieves 1.58-1.91$\times$ decode speedup while remaining within 1.4 ROUGE-2 points of the non-EE model. These speedups are 9-63% larger than EAGLE's across the evaluated model sizes, with each method measured against its own non-EE target.

Paper:
title: When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents
summary: An AI agent's decision not to act can itself become an attack surface. We study warning-induced over-abstention, an availability attack in which adversaries place fabricated risk warnings in low-trust content to prevent legitimate task completion. Our central premise is that safe abstention requires evaluating both the claimed risk and the authority of the evidence supporting it. We develop controlled counterfactual task variants that vary risk content, source provenance, and warning wording, and evaluate a Verify-Before-Abstain protocol that corroborates warnings against authoritative records or the underlying content. Across three model families and 51 injectable AgentAbstain task pairs, caution-first prompting amplifies the attack. For Gemini, induced over-abstention rises from $9.8\%$ to $86.3\%$, despite unchanged clean-task completion. Matched wording comparisons further reveal sensitivity to warning language, with substantial variation across models and environments. Provenance-aware verification improves legitimate completion, while forgery and sensitive-content controls expose its dependence on authoritative evidence and its limitations in preserving confidentiality. These results motivate evaluating agent safety through the justification for restraint, alongside the safety of actions taken.

Paper:
title: FedAdaVR: Adaptive Variance Reduction for Robust Federated Learning under Limited Client Participation
summary: Federated learning (FL) encounters substantial challenges due to heterogeneity, leading to gradient noise, client drift, and partial client participation errors, the last of which is the most pervasive but remains insufficiently addressed in current literature. In this paper, we propose FedAdaVR, a novel FL algorithm aimed at solving heterogeneity issues caused by partial client participation by incorporating an adaptive optimiser with a variance reduction technique. This method takes advantage of the most recent stored updates from clients, even when they are absent from the current training round, thereby emulating their presence. Furthermore, we propose FedAdaVR-Quant, a server-side memory compression variant that stores historical client updates in quantised form (while keeping client-server communication in full precision), reducing the server memory footprint of FedAdaVR by 50% (FP16), 75% (Int8), and 87.5% (Int4) while maintaining highly competitive, and occasionally superior model performance. We analyse the non-convex convergence behaviour of FedAdaVR with Adagrad and prove that our proposed framework eliminates the first-order partial client participation bias while improving monotonically with cohort size. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple vision and NLP datasets demonstrate that FedAdaVR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods.

Paper:
title: MARS: Towards High Goodput and Low KV Thrashing in Agent Serving under GPU Memory Constraints
summary: Self-hosted LLM agents offer greater control over sensitive data and model customization while avoiding per-request API fees. However, serving concurrent, multi-turn workflows within limited GPU memory makes it difficult to achieve high workflow-level goodput. In particular, as workflows accumulate context, their reusable key-value (KV) caches can easily outgrow GPU capacity, triggering repeated eviction and recovery, known as KV cache thrashing. This process consumes resources and delays workflow completion. Although existing approaches propose various methods, our motivation study shows that the evaluated baselines still incur substantial thrashing overhead or fail to address the workflow-level goodput issue.
  We present MARS, an agent serving system that coordinates workflow admission and in-engine scheduling to achieve high workflow-level goodput on memory-constrained devices while avoiding KV cache thrashing. Specifically, outside the engine, an admission controller selects root workflows using initial prefix footprint estimates and live KV availability, adapting admissions to memory pressure. Inside, an agent-centric scheduler prioritizes turn completion and coordinates prefill allocation with KV reclamation to reduce disruptive evictions. Across two models and three GPU configurations, MARS achieves 1.59x-7.56x mean end-to-end latency speedups over the fastest baseline. Integrated as the serving backend for OpenCode, Codex, and OpenHands, MARS further improves mean workflow completion time by 1.17x-1.87x.

Paper:
title: Mean field optimal Core Allocation across Malleable jobs
summary: Modern data centers and cloud computing clusters are increasingly running workloads composed of malleable jobs. A malleable job can be parallelized across any number of cores, yet the job typically exhibits diminishing marginal returns for each additional core on which it runs. Examples of malleable jobs include machine learning tasks, parallelized across multiple GPUs, and large-scale database queries, parallelized across multiple servers.
  Given the prevalence of malleable jobs, theoretical works have posed the problem of how to allocate a fixed number of cores across a stream of arriving malleable jobs so as to minimize the mean response time across jobs. We refer to this as the Core Allocation to Malleable jobs (CAM) problem. Although quite a few recent papers have been written on CAM, the problem remains challenging to solve optimally. In particular, prior theoretical work has only solved the CAM problem in very constrained cases.
  This paper takes a new approach to CAM, looking at the problem in the mean field asymptotic regime. In this regime, we are able to optimally solve a much more general instance of CAM. We derive two distinct mean field optimal policies, FW-CAM and GLAM. FW-CAM demonstrates a new intuition: in the mean field regime, individual job sizes are not relevant in finding an optimal policy. GLAM (Gittins-Like Allocation for Malleable jobs) is asymptotically optimal under certain common assumptions, and also serves as a good heuristic outside of the asymptotic regime by adapting dynamically to the current number of jobs in the system. Notably, none of the policies previously proposed in the literature are mean field optimal when jobs follow different speedup functions.

Paper:
title: BOA Constrictor: Squeezing Performance out of GPUs in the Cloud via Budget-Optimal Allocation
summary: The past decade has seen a dramatic increase in demand for GPUs to train Machine Learning (ML) models. Because it is prohibitively expensive for most organizations to build and maintain a large GPU cluster, organizations instead choose to rent GPUs from cloud providers. The customer is responsible for devising a policy for (i) deciding how many GPUs to rent at every moment in time to process a stream of ML training jobs and (ii) allocating the rented GPUs among the currently active jobs in the system. Because ML training jobs can be parallelized across different numbers of GPUs, the customer generally has many options for how many GPUs to use for each job. Allocating more GPUs to a single training job will cause the job to complete more quickly. However, the customer pays for each GPU-hour they use, and a training job receives a diminishing marginal benefit from running on additional GPUs. Hence, allocating too many GPUs to a single training job can dramatically increase the overall cost that the customer pays to the cloud provider. This gives rise to a cost-performance tradeoff that customers must balance when running training jobs in the cloud.
  To balance the cost-performance tradeoff, we develop BOA Constrictor, a new scheduler for ML training jobs which uses a Budget-Optimal Allocation (BOA) policy to squeeze the highest level of performance out of a cloud-deployed GPU cluster given a fixed budget constraint. We explicitly formulate the problem as a budget-constrained scheduling problem and derive the BOA policy which minimizes the average job completion time (JCT) of a stream of arriving jobs subject to the user's budget. For a given budget level, we demonstrate that BOA Constrictor can reduce average JCT by 1.6 times in small-scale implementation experiments and by 2 times in detailed, large-scale simulations compared to state-of-the-art heuristic based schedulers.

Paper:
title: What Does an RF Fingerprint Identify? A Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Hardware-Family-Associated and Unit-Level Signal
summary: RF fingerprinting benchmarks report how well a classifier separates transmitters, not whether that separability reflects the individual unit or its hardware family. We compare a benchmark's real hardware grouping with size-matched random groupings of the same devices, using calibrated, unclipped variational lower bounds under label-blind, device-level cross-fitting on devices never seen in training. On WiSig (OFDM Wi-Fi), the generation grouping exceeded all 999 matched random groupings (permutation p = 0.001, the resolution floor), although no grouping attained a positive certified bound, and the direction survives removing channel equalization. A preregistered replication on a LoRa corpus (chirp spread spectrum, three hardware models), with a front-end frozen on synthetic data, again exceeded all 999 (p = 0.001), and two sensitivity analyses judged by a reversal rule fixed in advance did not reverse the direction. This is a directional replication only: the excess magnitude reflects a miscalibrated null, the chain-rule decomposition leaves a residual of +0.296 bits, and capture order is undocumented. In a same-model corpus of 122 ESP32 radios, a temperature-calibrated held-out bound of +3.338 bits (label entropy 6.931 bits) indicates substantial device-specific identity, not separable from per-device capture-session effects; relying on the calibrated bound was decided after the uncalibrated bound changed sign. On synthetic transmitters a high-capacity convolutional decoder reaches 98.5% of a known 6-bit ceiling, and the audit protocol leaves chain-rule residuals of +0.072 bits (synthetic, fixed physical features) and +0.060 bits (WiSig, audit features). Two further corpora were excluded by preregistered ingest gates. Across WiSig and LoRa, hardware-family groupings consistently produced stronger identity-associated signal than size-matched random groupings.

Paper:
title: Hybrid FedGraph: An efficient hybrid federated learning algorithm using graph convolutional neural network
summary: Federated learning is an emerging paradigm for decentralized training of machine learning models on distributed clients, without revealing the data to the central server. Most existing works have focused on horizontal or vertical data distributions, where each client possesses different samples with shared features, or each client fully shares only sample indices, respectively. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a generalized algorithm, FedGraph, that introduces a graph convolutional neural network to capture feature-sharing information while learning features from a subset of clients. We also develop a simple but effective clustering algorithm that aggregates features produced by the deep neural networks of each client while preserving data privacy.

Paper:
title: OSCAR: Offline Spectral Covariance-Aware Rotation for 2-bit KV Cache Quantization
summary: INT2 KV-cache quantization is attractive for long-context LLM serving, yet making it both accurate and practical remains challenging. Data-oblivious rotations such as Hadamard transforms flatten channel outliers, but still degrade sharply at INT2 because they ignore how downstream attention queries the cache. We propose OSCAR, an ultra-low-bit KV-cache quantization method that estimates attention-aware covariance targets offline and uses them to derive fixed per-layer rotations and clipping thresholds. By aligning the quantization basis with the second-moment structures consumed by attention, OSCAR preserves attention fidelity at 2-bit precision. Beyond theoretical analysis under a frozen-error surrogate, we build a serving-ready OSCAR system with fused Triton write and decode kernels that preserve paged KV-cache layouts and prefix caching, integrating into modern serving engines such as SGLang and vLLM.
  We evaluate OSCAR on reasoning and coding benchmarks with generation traces of up to 32K tokens across five tasks. On Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-8B, OSCAR narrows the BF16 accuracy gap to 3.78 and 1.21 points, respectively, where Hadamard-only INT2 collapses, and matches BF16 within run-to-run variance on Qwen3-32B and GLM-4.7 (358B parameters). On RULER-NIAH up to 128K tokens, OSCAR substantially outperforms QuaRot-style INT2 across context lengths. System-wise, OSCAR compresses KV-cache memory by nearly $8\times$, boosts multi-request throughput by up to $7.8\times$ at large batch sizes within the same memory budget, and accelerates batch-size-1 decoding by up to $3.1\times$ over BF16 by cutting KV memory traffic.

Paper:
title: HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts.
  To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed directly without additional data rearrangement while maintaining transfer efficiency. We implement and evaluate HAWK on a system built with commercially available GPUs and NPUs, demonstrating performance within 7.88% of a GPU-only system under the same SLO constraints while achieving up to 1.26$\times$ higher power efficiency and 1.72$\times$ higher cost efficiency.

title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

title: AI Sandboxes: A Threat Model, Taxonomy, and Measurement Framework
summary: AI sandboxes produce evidence about systems that may act through software tools, networked devices, or physical actuators. Paper:
title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$μ$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering.
  We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).

Paper:
title: Security and Privacy Prompts in the Wild: What Users Ask LLMs and How LLMs Respond
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer users' information needs: users ask LLMs about the weather, pose educational questions, and consult them for legal assistance. One particularly understudied area is digital security and privacy (S&P), where users may seek LLMs' help on how to secure their online accounts or protect their computers from cyber attacks. To the best of our knowledge, no prior study has collected or analyzed the S&P questions users ask LLMs; prior research on LLM response quality relied on expert-authored S&P misconceptions or FAQs rather than user queries. Drawing from WildChat, a dataset of 3.2M user-LLM conversations collected in the wild, our study identifies 14,727 S&P prompts and categorizes them into nine categories covering a wide range of S&P topics. We sampled 450 S&P prompts, and performed a thematic analysis to characterize the S&P questions users ask LLMs. Separate from the thematic analysis, we curated 270 advice-seeking S&P prompts, where users ask for recommendations, guidance, or specific S&P information. We measured LLM response quality and consistency when posing each prompt to the LLMs 10 times. We found that commercial LLMs outperform open-weight models (GPT 5.5 provided "good enough" responses on 98% of prompts; Llama 4 on 47%). However, among prompts that received high-quality responses on average, commercial models sometimes produce semantically inconsistent responses across runs (some are contradictory, and others are different in specificity), thereby risking confusing or misleading users.

Paper:
title: Toward Optimal-Complexity Hash-Based Asynchronous MVBA with Optimal Resilience
summary: Multi-valued validated Byzantine agreement (MVBA), a fundamental primitive of distributed computing, allows $n$ processes to agree on a valid $\ell$-bit value, despite $t$ faulty processes behaving maliciously. Among hash-based solutions for the asynchronous setting with adaptive faults, the state-of-the-art HMVBA protocol achieves optimal $O(n^2)$ message complexity, (near-)optimal $O(n \ell + n^2 λ\log n)$ bit complexity, and optimal $O(1)$ time complexity. However, it only tolerates $t < \frac15 n$ failures. In contrast, the best-known optimally-resilient protocol, SQ, incurs a higher bit complexity of $O(n^2 \ell + n^3 λ)$. This poses a fundamental question: Can a hash-based protocol be designed for the asynchronous setting with adaptive faults that simultaneously achieves optimal complexity and optimal resilience?
  This paper takes a significant step toward answering this question. Namely, we introduce Reducer, an MVBA protocol that retains HMVBA's optimal complexity while improving its resilience to $t < \frac14 n$. Like HMVBA and SQ, Reducer relies exclusively on collision-resistant hash functions. A key innovation in Reducer's design is its internal use of strong multi-valued Byzantine agreement (SMBA), a new variant of Byzantine agreement we introduce and construct, which ensures that the decided value was proposed by a correct process. To further advance resilience toward the optimal one-third bound, we then propose Reducer++, an MVBA protocol that tolerates up to $t < (\frac13 - ε)n$ adaptive failures, for any fixed constant $ε> 0$. Unlike Reducer, Reducer++ does not rely on SMBA. Instead, it employs a novel approach involving hash functions modeled as random oracles to ensure termination. Reducer++ maintains constant time complexity, quadratic message complexity, and quasi-quadratic bit complexity, with constants dependent on $ε$.

Paper:
title: Reconstructing Fine-grained Memory Reuse Structure in GPU Kernels
summary: Optimizing GPU data movement requires knowing which instructions access the same data and across which execution scopes reuse occurs. Existing profilers can attribute memory behavior to individual instructions but do not expose the reuse relations among them, while aliasing, dynamic indexing, and runtime parameters prevent static analysis from establishing these relations in general. Cycle-level simulation can reconstruct such relations, but at costs prohibitive for production workloads. We introduce two abstractions for representing this structure: Topological Distance, which labels each dynamic memory access with the smallest execution scope (thread, warp, block, or grid) containing its most recent reuse, and PCDepGraph, which organizes these labels into a PC-level graph of the kernel's memory reuse structure. Defined over logical execution scopes rather than transient hardware state, the representation remains stable across runs and GPU targets while directly indicating the sharing scope that candidate optimization mechanisms must cover. Our tool, cuVein, reconstructs PCDepGraph directly from optimized binaries, without sampling, at generally under 10x overhead. Across HPC and AI workloads on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and H100, optimizations guided by PCDepGraph eliminate up to 90.18% of memory instructions and yield up to 2.84x kernel speedup; reuse-scope distributions remain consistent across platforms, supporting that the representation captures program structure rather than transient hardware behavior.

Paper:
title: CellularS2-Bench: A Staged, Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Cellular Network Security Reasoning
summary: Cellular networks are critical infrastructure supporting billions of worldwide users and safety- and mission-critical services. Vulnerabilities in cellular networks can therefore cause service disruption, privacy breaches, and broad societal harm, motivating growing efforts to analyze 3GPP specifications that define required device and operator behavior. However, existing benchmarks for this domain share three systematic deficiencies: they rely on LLM-generated entries without expert verification, they do not require faithful interpretation of normative language, reasoning across cross-referenced clauses, and verifiable conclusions grounded in multimodal evidence such as tables and figures, and they do not evaluate security reasoning over end-to-end protocol behavior. To address these gaps, we present CellularS2-Bench, a staged benchmark. CellularS2-Bench covers core control-plane specifications, processing over 1,866 paragraphs, 22,033 sentences, 424 figures, and 248 tables. It comprises 13,851 questions and instances across three progressive stages, of which 10,269 (74.14%) are newly constructed from 3GPP specifications and 43 real-world vulnerabilities. Beyond newly constructed tasks, CellularS2-Bench integrates and corrects 3,582 (25.86%) instances from 7 prior datasets to broaden task coverage. To establish a reproducible baseline on CellularS2-Bench, we introduce CellularS2-ARI, a unified Adapt-Retrieve-Integrate framework for systematic understanding and specification-driven security analysis of 3GPP specifications. Together, they establish an accessible and reproducible foundation for quantifying progress in specification understanding and security reasoning in cellular network security.

Paper:
title: Robust & Scalable Website Fingerprinting via Minimal DRAM Traffic
summary: Website fingerprinting attacks infer websites visited by users and threaten their privacy. These attacks are classified as on-path, which monitor network traffic, and co-located, which exploit shared system resources. Existing co-located attacks, such as sweep-counting and loop-counting, achieve over 90% accuracy but suffer significant performance degradation on many-core systems. Loop-counting accuracy drops from 93% on 8 cores to 50% on 24 cores, while sweep-counting accuracy decreases from 84% to 45% across multiple Core Complex Dies (CCDs). To address these limitations, we propose memory-chasing, a scalable website fingerprinting attack that exploits DRAM traffic interference through pointer-chasing traversals with minimal interference. By counting DRAM accesses over fixed intervals, the attack generates distinctive traces for website classification. Evaluated on the top 50 websites, memory-chasing achieves 96% accuracy on a 24-core system, 86% across multiple CCDs, 80% across multiple sockets, and 97% in an open-world setting. Extensive evaluation across hardware configurations, browsers, operating systems, isolation mechanisms, system noise, and countermeasures demonstrates its robustness and scalability.

Paper:
title: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle Aided Computation
summary: Incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) allows a prover to maintain a short proof that can be efficiently updated after each computation step, without retaining or recomputing the preceding execution. Standard IVC schemes do not directly address a crucial feature of AI tasks: their dependence on external information and expertise.
  We construct IVC schemes for oracle-aided computations under the LWE assumption by first constructing SNARGs, and then extending them to IVC. We consider the following two settings, where below, k is the security parameter, n is the input length, and T, S, and Q are the time, space, and oracle-query bounds.
  1. Robust computations: For bounded-space computations, including non-deterministic computations, in which every accepting purported execution on a false input contains at least an eps-fraction of incorrect oracle answers, we construct privately verifiable SNARGs and IVC. Public parameters, private verification keys, and proofs have length poly(k ,S, log T,1/eps), and verification uses O(k/eps) oracle calls. We complement this result with a lower bound ruling out (deterministic) publicly verifiable SNARGs and IVCs with public parameters of length o(n), and o(Q) verifier oracle queries.
  2. Signed oracles: For oracles that digitally sign their query-answer pairs, we construct publicly verifiable SNARGs and IVC without a robustness assumption, and with oracle-free setup and verification. Public parameters and proofs have length poly(k,S,log T). For deterministic computations with oracle query and answer lengths poly(k,log T), we remove the dependence on S, obtaining public parameter and proof lengths poly(k,log T).
  All our constructions have adaptive completeness and soundness.
